decks.title: Structure of Atom — Part 1: Atomic models, radiation and the Bohr model
goals: Describe the subatomic particles and the Thomson and Rutherford models with their limitations
Use c = νλ and E = hν for electromagnetic radiation and the photoelectric effect
Interpret the hydrogen line spectrum and apply Bohr’s model to energies, radii and transitions

slides.heading: Structure of Atom
slides.body_md: Part 1 — from the electron and the nucleus to the first quantum model of the atom.

visual.alt: Table of charge and mass of the electron, proton and neutron

slides.narration: Welcome. Everything around us is built from atoms, and atoms from three particles: the electron, the proton and the neutron. In this part we follow how scientists discovered them, why the early models failed, how light carries energy in packets, and how Niels Bohr used that idea to explain the colours emitted by hydrogen.

slides.heading: Discovery of subatomic particles
slides.body_md: Cathode rays showed that atoms contain **electrons**; canal rays revealed **protons**; Chadwick found the **neutron** in 1932. Thomson measured the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron, $e/m_\text{e} = 1.76 \times 10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$, and Millikan’s oil-drop experiment gave its charge.

rows: Cathode rays deflected by electric and magnetic fields

visual.alt: Table of who discovered each subatomic particle and the evidence

slides.narration: Cathode rays in a discharge tube bent towards a positive plate, so they carry negative charge. Thomson measured how much they bend and found the charge to mass ratio of the electron. Millikan then measured the charge itself with tiny oil drops. Protons came from canal rays, and Chadwick discovered the neutron in nineteen thirty-two by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles.

slides.heading: Thomson’s model
slides.body_md: Thomson pictured the atom as a positive sphere with electrons embedded like seeds in a watermelon or raisins in a pudding: **electrically neutral**, with charge spread uniformly. It could not explain what Rutherford observed.

visual.alt: Table comparing Thomson’s model with Rutherford’s nuclear model

slides.narration: Thomson’s first model of the atom had positive charge spread through the whole sphere, with electrons embedded in it like raisins in a pudding. The atom is neutral overall. This picture was simple, but it predicted that fast alpha particles should pass through with only tiny deflections. The experiment that tested this prediction overturned it.

slides.heading: Rutherford’s alpha-scattering experiment
slides.body_md: A narrow beam of $\alpha$-particles was fired at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were deflected through small angles, and **very few rebounded**.

slides.narration: Look at the picture. Alpha particles from the source strike a very thin gold foil. Nearly all go straight through, a few are bent slightly, and very few bounce almost straight back. Rutherford said it was like firing a shell at tissue paper and seeing it come back. The only explanation was a tiny, heavy, positive centre in every atom.

slides.heading: Rutherford’s conclusions and limitations
slides.body_md: The atom is mostly **empty space**; the positive charge and almost all the mass are in a tiny **nucleus** (about $10^{-15}$ m across, compared with an atom of about $10^{-10}$ m); electrons move around it. But classical physics says such an electron should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, and the model could not explain **line spectra**.

rows: A few deflected through large angles
Atom is stable and gives line spectra
Not explained: needed a new model

visual.alt: Table linking Rutherford’s observations to inferences and an unresolved problem

slides.narration: Each observation leads to an inference. No deflection means empty space, large deflection means concentrated positive charge, and a rebound means a small, heavy nucleus. The nucleus is about one hundred thousand times smaller than the atom. But there were two problems: a circling electron should lose energy and fall into the nucleus, and the model gave no explanation for sharp spectral lines.

slides.heading: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes
slides.body_md: **Atomic number** $Z$ = number of protons; **mass number** $A = Z +$ number of neutrons. **Isotopes** have the same $Z$ but different $A$; **isobars** have the same $A$ but different $Z$.

visual.alt: Table of isotopes of hydrogen and a pair of isobars

slides.narration: The atomic number counts protons and identifies the element. The mass number counts protons plus neutrons. Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are isotopes; hydrogen has three, protium, deuterium and tritium. Atoms with the same mass number but different atomic numbers, such as argon forty and calcium forty, are called isobars.

slides.heading: Electromagnetic radiation
slides.body_md:
Light is a wave of oscillating electric and magnetic fields travelling at $c = 3.0 	imes 10^{8}\ 	ext{m s}^{-1}$ in vacuum. Frequency $
u$ and wavelength $\lambda$ are linked by $c = 
u\lambda$; **wavenumber** $ ar{
u} = 1/\lambda$.

visual.alt: Table of regions of the electromagnetic spectrum with wavelength and frequency ranges

slides.narration: Light is an electromagnetic wave. In vacuum every wave travels at the same speed, so frequency and wavelength are inversely related: the shorter the wavelength, the higher the frequency. The table runs from radio waves of low frequency through visible light to X-rays of very high frequency. Wavenumber is simply the reciprocal of wavelength.

slides.heading: Worked example: frequency, wavelength and wavenumber
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) A mobile network uses radiation of frequency $1800\ \text{MHz}$. Find its wavelength. (b) Find the frequency of orange light of wavelength $600\ \text{nm}$. (c) Find the wavenumber of the orange light in m⁻¹. ($c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$)

**(a)** $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{\nu} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.8 \times 10^{9}} \approx 0.167$ m.

**(b)** $\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{6.00 \times 10^{-7}} = 5.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

**(c)** $\bar{\nu} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{6.00 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 1.67 \times 10^{6}$ m⁻¹.

nodes.label: Convert to SI: MHz to Hz, nm to m

visual.alt: Flow for frequency, wavelength and wavenumber calculations: convert to SI units, apply c equals nu lambda

slides.narration: Always convert to SI units first: megahertz to hertz and nanometres to metres. Then divide the speed of light by the frequency to get wavelength, or by the wavelength to get frequency. Orange light of six hundred nanometres has a frequency of five times ten to the fourteen hertz. Wavenumber is one divided by the wavelength in metres.

slides.heading: Planck’s quantum theory and the photoelectric effect
slides.body_md:
Energy is emitted or absorbed in packets, **quanta**: $E = h
u = hc/\lambda$, $h = 6.626 	imes 10^{-34}\ 	ext{J s}$. In the **photoelectric effect** light above a **threshold frequency** $
u_0$ ejects electrons: $h
u = h
u_0 + 	frac{1}{2}m_	ext{e}v^2$.

rows: No electrons below $\nu_0$, however intense the light
One photon gives its whole energy to one electron; $h\nu < h\nu_0$ is too little
Kinetic energy rises with frequency, not intensity
Should need time to build up energy

visual.alt: Table of photoelectric observations that a wave theory cannot explain and the photon explanation

slides.narration: Max Planck proposed that energy comes in packets called quanta, with energy equal to Planck’s constant times frequency. Einstein used this to explain the photoelectric effect. Light below a threshold frequency ejects no electrons however bright it is, because a single photon is too weak. Above it, extra energy becomes kinetic energy. Brighter light of the same frequency just ejects more electrons.

slides.heading: Worked example: photon energy and photoelectron energy
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Ultraviolet light of wavelength $300\ \text{nm}$ falls on a metal whose threshold wavelength is $500\ \text{nm}$. Find (a) the energy of one photon, (b) the threshold energy and (c) the kinetic energy of an ejected electron. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$)

**(a)** $E = hc/\lambda = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8} / 3.00 \times 10^{-7} = 6.63 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

**(b)** $E_0 = hc/\lambda_0 = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8} / 5.00 \times 10^{-7} = 3.98 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

**(c)** $\text{KE} = E - E_0 = 6.63 \times 10^{-19} - 3.98 \times 10^{-19} = 2.65 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

visual.alt: Table of photon energy, threshold energy and photoelectron kinetic energy

slides.narration: The photon carries Planck’s constant times the speed of light divided by the wavelength. Shorter wavelength means more energy. The metal holds on to its electrons with a threshold energy, found the same way from the threshold wavelength. The difference between the two energies is what is left over as kinetic energy of the ejected electron.

slides.heading: The hydrogen line spectrum
slides.body_md: Excited hydrogen emits only certain wavelengths, a **line spectrum**. They fit $\bar{\nu} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^{2}}\right)$ with $n_2 > n_1$. Each value of $n_1$ gives a **series**.

visual.alt: Table of hydrogen spectral series with lower level, upper levels and spectral region

slides.narration: A glowing hydrogen tube does not give a rainbow but a few sharp coloured lines. Their wavelengths fit a simple formula, the Rydberg equation, with two whole numbers. Fixing the lower number gives a whole series: Lyman in the ultraviolet, Balmer in the visible, then Paschen, Brackett and Pfund in the infrared. A good model of the atom had to explain this pattern.

slides.heading: Bohr’s model of the hydrogen atom
slides.body_md: (1) Electrons move in fixed **stationary orbits** without radiating. (2) Orbits have angular momentum $m_\text{e}vr = nh/2\pi$. (3) Light is emitted or absorbed only when an electron jumps between orbits: $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = h\nu$.

visual.alt: Table of Bohr energies and radii of the first three levels of hydrogen

slides.narration: Bohr made three bold postulates. Electrons travel only in certain allowed orbits and do not radiate while in them. Each orbit has a fixed energy, negative because the electron is bound, and equal to minus two point one eight times ten to the minus eighteen joule divided by n squared. Light is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps, with energy equal to the difference between two levels.

slides.heading: Energy levels and spectral series
slides.body_md: Transitions **down** to $n = 1$, 2 or 3 give the Lyman, Balmer and Paschen series; the lines come from the **differences** between levels, which is why the spectrum is discrete.

slides.narration: This diagram is drawn to scale. The levels crowd together as n gets larger, and at the top the electron is free. Each arrow is a transition that emits one photon. All arrows ending on the lowest level form the Lyman series, in the ultraviolet; those ending on the second level form the Balmer series, in the visible; and so on. The energy gap fixes the wavelength of each line.

slides.heading: Worked example: a Bohr transition
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For hydrogen find (a) the energy of the $n = 2$ level, (b) the wavelength of the line produced when an electron falls from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$, and (c) the energy needed to ionise one mole of hydrogen atoms in the ground state. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $N_\text{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)

**(a)** $E_2 = -2.18 \times 10^{-18} / 4 = -5.45 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

**(b)** $\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,(1/4 - 1/9) = 3.03 \times 10^{-19}$ J, so $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{3.03 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 6.56 \times 10^{-7}$ m $= 656$ nm (red).

**(c)** Ionisation: $n = 1 \to \infty$ needs $2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J per atom, that is $2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.31 \times 10^{6}$ J mol⁻¹ $= 1.31 \times 10^{3}$ kJ mol⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the results of the Bohr worked example

slides.narration: Divide the ground-state energy by n squared for any level. A transition emits a photon whose energy is the difference between the two levels, and dividing Planck’s constant times the speed of light by that energy gives the wavelength, here red light of six hundred fifty-six nanometres. To ionise hydrogen, lift the electron from the first level to infinity, then scale by Avogadro’s number to get kilojoules per mole.

slides.heading: The quantum mechanical atom
slides.body_md: Part 2 — electrons as waves, orbitals instead of orbits, and how electrons fill them.

visual.alt: Flow of the topics in Part 2: limits of Bohr model, matter waves and uncertainty, orbitals and quantum numbers, configuration

slides.narration: Bohr’s model could not explain atoms with more than one electron, and it treated the electron only as a particle. In this part we see that matter also behaves like a wave, that we cannot know exactly where an electron is, and that this leads to orbitals described by four quantum numbers. Finally we use these ideas to write the electronic configuration of any atom.

slides.heading: Limitations of the Bohr model
slides.body_md: Bohr’s model works for H, He⁺, Li²⁺ but fails elsewhere.

rows: Cannot explain splitting of lines in a magnetic or electric field (Zeeman and Stark effects)
Treats it only as a particle in a fixed orbit
Gives exact position and speed, which cannot be known together

visual.alt: Table of the limitations of Bohr’s model of the atom

slides.narration: Bohr’s model works well for hydrogen and one-electron ions such as helium plus. It fails for atoms with more electrons, cannot explain why spectral lines split in magnetic or electric fields, treats the electron only as a particle, and gives exact orbits that violate the uncertainty principle. A new theory based on the wave nature of matter was needed.

slides.heading: Dual nature of matter: de Broglie’s relation
slides.body_md: de Broglie proposed that a moving particle has a wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{h}{p}$. It is significant only for **microscopic** particles; for large objects $\lambda$ is far too small to detect.

visual.alt: Table of de Broglie wavelengths of an electron, a cricket ball and a bullet

slides.narration: Louis de Broglie suggested that if light can behave as a particle, matter can behave as a wave, with wavelength equal to Planck’s constant divided by momentum. For an electron the wavelength is comparable with the size of an atom, so it matters. For a cricket ball or a bullet it is smaller than anything we can measure, so everyday objects appear to have no wave nature.

slides.heading: Worked example: de Broglie wavelength
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the de Broglie wavelength of (a) a neutron moving at $2200\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ($m = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}$ kg) and (b) a $50\ \text{g}$ bullet moving at $300\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)

**(a)** $\lambda = h/mv = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} / (1.675 \times 10^{-27} \times 2200) = 1.80 \times 10^{-10}$ m $= 180$ pm.

**(b)** $m = 0.050$ kg, so $\lambda = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} / (0.050 \times 300) = 4.4 \times 10^{-35}$ m.

visual.alt: Table comparing the wavelengths of a neutron and a bullet and whether they are detectable

slides.narration: Divide Planck’s constant by the momentum, mass times speed, taking care to use kilograms. The slow neutron has a wavelength about the spacing between atoms in a crystal, so crystals can diffract it. The bullet’s wavelength is about thirty orders of magnitude smaller than the nucleus, so its wave nature is completely unobservable.

slides.heading: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle
slides.body_md: It is impossible to know simultaneously and exactly both the **position** and the **momentum** of a microscopic particle: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$, or $\Delta x \cdot \Delta v \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi m}$. This rules out the idea of definite orbits.

visual.alt: Table of minimum velocity uncertainty for an electron and a cricket ball

slides.narration: Heisenberg showed that the more precisely we fix an electron’s position, the less precisely we can know its momentum, and the product of the two uncertainties cannot fall below Planck’s constant divided by four pi. For an electron the unavoidable uncertainty in speed is enormous, so a definite orbit makes no sense. For a ball it is far too small to notice.

slides.heading: Worked example: uncertainty in speed
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The position of an electron in an atom is known to within $5.0 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{m}$. Find the minimum uncertainty in its speed. ($m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$)

**Step 1.** $\Delta v \ge h / (4\pi m \Delta x)$.

**Step 2.** $4\pi m \Delta x = 4 \times 3.142 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-11} = 5.72 \times 10^{-40}$.

**Step 3.** $\Delta v = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{5.72 \times 10^{-40}} \approx 1.16 \times 10^{6}$ m s⁻¹.

visual.alt: Flow for calculating the minimum uncertainty in velocity from the uncertainty in position

slides.narration: Rearrange the uncertainty relation to give the uncertainty in speed. Multiply four pi by the mass and the uncertainty in position, then divide Planck’s constant by that number. The result, more than a million metres per second, is comparable with the speed of the electron itself, which shows that we cannot talk about a precise path for an electron inside an atom.

slides.heading: Quick check: matter waves
slides.body_md: Compare the wave nature of two particles.
slides.narration: Quick check. Wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum, so compare the masses or speeds.

slides.heading: Orbitals: the quantum mechanical model
slides.body_md: Schrödinger’s equation gives wave functions $\psi$ whose squares $\psi^2$ give the **probability density** of finding an electron. An **orbital** is a region with a high probability of finding the electron; it is **not** a path.

visual.alt: Table comparing a Bohr orbit with a quantum mechanical orbital

slides.narration: In the quantum mechanical model we solve Schrödinger’s equation for the electron’s wave function. The square of the wave function tells us how likely we are to find the electron at each point. An orbital is the region where that probability is high. It is not a path, and each orbital can hold at most two electrons. The model works for all atoms.

slides.heading: The four quantum numbers
slides.body_md: Each electron in an atom is described by four numbers: **n** (shell: size and energy), **l** (subshell: shape), **mₗ** (orientation) and **mₛ** (spin).

rows: 0 to n − 1 (s, p, d, f for 0, 1, 2, 3)

visual.alt: Table of the four quantum numbers with allowed values and meaning

slides.narration: Four quantum numbers fix the state of an electron. The principal quantum number n sets the shell and the size. The azimuthal number l runs from zero to n minus one and sets the shape: s, p, d and f for zero to three. The magnetic number gives the orientation, with two l plus one values. The spin number is plus or minus one half.

slides.heading: Worked example: counting orbitals and electrons
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For the shell $n = 3$: (a) list the subshells, (b) count the orbitals, (c) find the maximum number of electrons. (d) Is the set $n = 3, l = 3, m_l = 0$ allowed?

**(a)** $l = 0, 1, 2$: 3s, 3p, 3d.

**(b)** $(2l + 1)$: $1 + 3 + 5 = 9$ orbitals $= n^{2}$.

**(c)** Two electrons per orbital: $2 \times 9 = 18 = 2n^{2}$.

**(d)** No: $l$ cannot exceed $n - 1 = 2$.

visual.alt: Table of subshells of the third shell with orbitals and electrons

slides.narration: For the third shell, l can be zero, one or two, so there are three subshells. They hold one, three and five orbitals, nine in all, which is n squared. With two electrons per orbital, the shell holds eighteen electrons, which is two n squared. A value of l equal to three is not allowed for n equal to three, because l must be less than n.

slides.heading: Shapes of orbitals and nodes
slides.body_md: **s** orbitals are spherical; **p** orbitals are dumbbells along $x$, $y$, $z$ (three per subshell); **d** orbitals have four lobes (or two lobes and a ring), five per subshell. A **node** is where $\psi^2 = 0$: radial nodes $= n - l - 1$, angular nodes $= l$, total nodes $= n - 1$.

visual.alt: Table of radial, angular and total nodes for six orbitals

slides.narration: An s orbital is a sphere, a p orbital is a dumbbell with a nodal plane through the nucleus, and a d orbital has two angular nodes. A node is a place where the electron is never found. The number of angular nodes equals l, the number of radial nodes equals n minus l minus one, and the total number of nodes is n minus one.

slides.body_md: The lobes of different sign are shown in different colours; the **nodal planes** and **spherical nodes** are where the wave function changes sign.

slides.heading: Energy of orbitals and the Aufbau principle
slides.body_md: In a many-electron atom energy depends on $n$ **and** $l$. Orbitals fill in order of increasing $(n + l)$; if equal, the lower $n$ fills first. **Aufbau principle:** electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbitals available.

visual.alt: Table of n plus l values and the order of filling of orbitals up to 4p

slides.narration: In an atom with many electrons, an orbital’s energy depends on both n and l. We fill the lowest first, using the rule n plus l. Four s has n plus l equal to four, lower than three d at five, so four s fills before three d. When two orbitals tie, the one with the smaller n fills first. The order is one s, two s, two p, three s, three p, four s, three d, four p.

slides.heading: Pauli exclusion principle and Hund’s rule
slides.body_md: **Pauli:** no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most **two** electrons with opposite spins. **Hund:** degenerate orbitals of a subshell are filled **singly** with parallel spins before any pairing.

rows: No two electrons share all four quantum numbers

visual.alt: Table of the Aufbau, Pauli and Hund rules with consequences

slides.narration: Two more rules complete the filling. Pauli’s exclusion principle says no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons and they must spin in opposite directions. Hund’s rule says that in a subshell like p, each orbital gets one electron before any gets a second, and the single electrons spin in the same direction.

slides.heading: Box diagrams and the exceptional cases
slides.body_md: Nitrogen: three unpaired 2p electrons (Hund). Oxygen: one pair and two unpaired. **Chromium** and **copper** deviate from the simple order to reach half-filled or completely filled 3d.

slides.narration: In the box diagram, each box is an orbital and each arrow an electron. Nitrogen puts one electron in each of the three p boxes. Oxygen must pair one. slides.heading: Worked example: writing configurations
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the ground-state configurations and the number of unpaired electrons: (a) $\ce{Cl-}$ (Z = 17), (b) Fe (Z = 26), (c) $\ce{Fe^3+}$.

**(a)** Cl: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^5$; adding one electron gives $\ce{Cl-}$: $[\text{Ne}]\,3s^2 3p^6$, with **0** unpaired electrons.

**(b)** Fe: $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6 4s^2$; the six 3d electrons occupy five boxes, so **4** are unpaired.

**(c)** $\ce{Fe^3+}$: the two 4s electrons leave first, then one 3d: $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$, **5** unpaired electrons (half-filled).

visual.alt: Table of configurations and unpaired electrons for chloride, iron and iron three plus

slides.narration: Start with the atom’s configuration, then add or remove electrons for ions. Chloride gains one electron and has a full outer shell, so none are unpaired. Iron has six electrons in three d, so four are unpaired. When iron forms positive ions, the four s electrons leave first, then three d, so iron three plus has five unpaired electrons in a half-filled three d subshell.

slides.heading: Exceptional configurations: chromium and copper
slides.body_md: Cr is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1$, not $3d^4 4s^2$; Cu is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1$, not $3d^9 4s^2$. **Half-filled** and **completely filled** subshells are extra stable because of symmetrical distribution and greater **exchange energy**.

visual.alt: Table of expected and observed configurations of chromium and copper with the reason

slides.narration: Two famous exceptions. Chromium would be expected to have four electrons in three d and two in four s, but one electron moves so that three d is exactly half-filled. Copper moves one electron to make three d completely filled. Half-filled and filled subshells are especially stable, because the electrons are symmetrically distributed and there is greater exchange energy.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: de Broglie: $\lambda = h/mv$; Heisenberg: $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge h/4\pi$.
Orbital: region of high probability; four quantum numbers n, l, mₗ, mₛ.
Radial nodes $= n - l - 1$; angular nodes $= l$; total $= n - 1$; orbitals in shell $= n^2$.
Filling: Aufbau ($n + l$), Pauli (two per orbital), Hund (singly first).
Cr is $3d^5 4s^1$ and Cu is $3d^{10} 4s^1$ because half-filled and filled subshells are extra stable.

visual.alt: Summary table of counting formulae for shells, subshells and nodes

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Matter has a wavelength given by Planck’s constant over momentum, and the uncertainty principle forbids exact orbits. The electron in an atom is described by an orbital and four quantum numbers. Electrons fill orbitals by the Aufbau principle, Pauli’s exclusion principle and Hund’s rule, with chromium and copper as the standard exceptions.

For ions, remove electrons from the highest n first (4s before 3d).
Show orbital box diagrams to argue Hund’s rule.

sections.body_md:
**Electron** (Thomson, cathode rays; $e/m = 1.76 \times 10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$; charge by Millikan), **proton** (canal rays) and **neutron** (Chadwick, 1932). Atomic number $Z$ = protons; mass number $A$ = protons + neutrons. **Isotopes:** same $Z$, different $A$. **Isobars:** same $A$, different $Z$.

**Thomson:** positive sphere with embedded electrons. **Rutherford** ($\alpha$-scattering on gold foil): most particles undeflected (empty space), few deflected (concentrated positive charge), very few rebound (small dense nucleus, about $10^{-15}$ m versus atom $10^{-10}$ m). Limitations: a circling electron should spiral inward; line spectra unexplained.

Rydberg: $\bar{\nu} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\,(1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2)$. Series: Lyman ($n_1 = 1$, UV), Balmer (2, visible), Paschen (3, IR), Brackett (4), Pfund (5).

sections.heading: 4. Wave nature of matter and uncertainty
sections.body_md:
**de Broglie:** $\lambda = h/mv$; significant for electrons and other microscopic particles, negligible for a cricket ball ($\sim 10^{-34}$ m). **Heisenberg:** $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge h/4\pi$; for an electron confined to about an atom the uncertainty in speed is of the order $10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so definite orbits cannot exist.

**Orbital:** region of high probability $\psi^2$ of finding the electron; each holds at most two electrons.

key_terms.definition_md: The wavelength $h/mv$ associated with a moving particle.
A region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is high.

sections.heading: 5. Quantum numbers and orbital shapes
sections.body_md:
**n** = 1, 2, 3 … (shell); **l** = 0 to $n-1$ (s, p, d, f); **mₗ** = $-l$ to $+l$ ($2l + 1$ orbitals); **mₛ** = ±½. A shell holds $n^2$ orbitals and $2n^2$ electrons.

**Shapes:** s spherical; p dumbbell (3 orbitals); d four-lobed or lobes with ring (5 orbitals). **Nodes:** radial $= n - l - 1$; angular $= l$; total $= n - 1$.

key_terms.definition_md: $l$: fixes the shape of the subshell (0 s, 1 p, 2 d, 3 f).
A region where the probability of finding the electron is zero.

sections.heading: 6. Electronic configuration
sections.body_md:
**Aufbau:** fill in order of increasing $n + l$ (lower $n$ first on a tie): 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s … **Pauli:** no two electrons share all four quantum numbers (max two per orbital, opposite spins). **Hund:** fill degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins first.

**Exceptions:** Cr $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1$ and Cu $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1$ (half-filled and filled subshells are extra stable: symmetry and exchange energy). Cations lose the outermost (highest $n$) electrons first: Fe³⁺ is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$.

key_terms.definition_md: Electrons fill the lowest-energy available orbitals first.
No two electrons in an atom have the same set of four quantum numbers.
Degenerate orbitals are singly occupied, with parallel spins, before pairing.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using nm or MHz directly instead of converting to SI units.
- Forgetting that only frequency (not intensity) decides the kinetic energy of photoelectrons.
- Writing positive energies for bound electron levels.
- Allowing l = n, or mₗ outside −l to +l.
- Writing Cr as 3d⁴ 4s² or Cu as 3d⁹ 4s².
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s electrons when forming ions.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a definition, value or single rule.
- Numericals (2–3 marks): formula (1), substitution with SI units (1), answer with unit (1).
- Quantum-number questions: allowed values (1), count of orbitals (1), reasoning (1).
- Configuration answers: correct order (1), reason for exceptions (1).

cards.front_md: What did most alpha particles do in Rutherford’s experiment, and what does it show?
cards.back_md: They passed straight through: the atom is mostly empty space.

cards.front_md: What did the rebound of very few alpha particles show?
cards.back_md: A small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

cards.front_md: Two limitations of Rutherford’s model?
cards.back_md: It cannot explain the stability of the atom or line spectra.

cards.front_md: Isotopes versus isobars?
cards.back_md: Isotopes: same Z, different A. Isobars: same A, different Z.

cards.front_md: Relation between speed, frequency and wavelength of light?
cards.back_md: $c = \nu\lambda$

cards.front_md: Planck’s relation?
cards.back_md: $E = h\nu$, with $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s.

cards.front_md: What is wavenumber?
cards.back_md: $\bar{\nu} = 1/\lambda$, in m⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Photoelectric equation?
cards.back_md: $h\nu = h\nu_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}m_\text{e}v^2$

cards.front_md: What does increasing the intensity of light do in the photoelectric effect?
cards.back_md: Increases the number of electrons emitted, not their kinetic energy.

cards.front_md: Which photon has more energy: red or violet?
cards.back_md: Violet (shorter wavelength, higher frequency).

cards.front_md: Bohr energy of hydrogen level n?
Bohr radius of hydrogen orbit n?
Which series is visible in hydrogen?
cards.back_md: Balmer (electron falls to n = 2).

cards.front_md: Rydberg formula?
Number of spectral lines when an electron falls from level n?
cards.back_md: $n(n-1)/2$ if all transitions occur.

cards.front_md: Limitations of Bohr’s model?
cards.back_md: Fails for many-electron atoms, line splitting in fields, ignores wave nature and uncertainty.

cards.front_md: de Broglie relation?
cards.back_md: $\lambda = h/mv$

cards.front_md: Why can’t we see the wave nature of a cricket ball?
cards.back_md: Its wavelength (about 10⁻³⁴ m) is far too small to detect.

cards.front_md: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle?
cards.back_md: $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge h/4\pi$

cards.front_md: Orbit versus orbital?
cards.back_md: Orbit: fixed circular path (Bohr). Orbital: region of high probability of finding the electron.

cards.front_md: Allowed values of l and mₗ?
cards.back_md: l = 0 to n − 1; mₗ = −l to +l.

cards.front_md: How many orbitals and electrons in shell n?
cards.back_md: $n^2$ orbitals and $2n^2$ electrons.

cards.front_md: Radial and angular nodes?
cards.back_md: Radial nodes = n − l − 1; angular nodes = l.

cards.front_md: Shapes of s, p and d orbitals?
cards.back_md: Spherical; dumbbell; four-lobed (or two lobes with a ring).

cards.front_md: Aufbau (n + l) order from 4s?
Pauli exclusion principle?
cards.back_md: No two electrons in an atom have the same four quantum numbers.

cards.front_md: Hund’s rule?
cards.back_md: Fill degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.

cards.front_md: Configurations of Cr and Cu?
cards.back_md: Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹. Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.

cards.front_md: Why are half-filled and filled subshells extra stable?
cards.back_md: Symmetrical distribution and greater exchange energy.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: which electrons does an atom lose first?
cards.back_md: Those of the highest n, so 4s before 3d.

questions.stem_md: In Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment, the rebound of a very few alpha particles showed that:

options.text_md: electrons are embedded uniformly in a positive sphere
the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
electrons move in fixed circular orbits of definite energy
the atom is completely hollow with no positive charge

questions.solution_md: A particle can only be turned back by a very small, dense, positively charged centre — option (b). A uniform positive sphere (a) would deflect alpha particles only slightly.

questions.stem_md: The numbers of electrons, protons and neutrons in $^{35}\text{Cl}^{-}$ (Z = 17) are, respectively:
questions.solution_md: Protons = Z = 17; neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18; the chloride ion has one extra electron, 17 + 1 = 18 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The species $^{40}\text{Ar}$, $^{40}\text{K}$ and $^{40}\text{Ca}$ (atomic numbers 18, 19 and 20) are:
questions.solution_md: They share the same mass number (40) but have different atomic numbers, so they are isobars — option (d). Isotopes (a) would share the atomic number.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Most alpha particles passed through the gold foil without deflection.

**Reason (R):** Most of the volume of an atom is empty space.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Because the nucleus is tiny, most alpha particles never come close to one and go straight through; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Thomson’s plum-pudding model could explain the large-angle scattering of alpha particles.
questions.solution_md: False. A uniformly spread positive charge would deflect alpha particles only slightly; the large-angle scattering needed a concentrated nucleus (Rutherford).

questions.stem_md: Match each scientist with the contribution to atomic structure.

match_right.text_md: Proposed a small, dense, positively charged nucleus
Proposed that moving particles have a wavelength
Proposed quantised stationary orbits for hydrogen
Measured the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron

questions.solution_md: Thomson: e/m of the electron; Rutherford: the nucleus; Bohr: stationary orbits; de Broglie: matter waves.

questions.stem_md: State one observation of Rutherford’s experiment that Thomson’s model could not explain, and say what feature of Rutherford’s model accounts for it.

answer.model_answer_md: Thomson’s model could not explain why a very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles or rebounded. Rutherford’s model places all the positive charge and nearly all the mass in a tiny nucleus, which can strongly repel a fast alpha particle that passes very close to it.

questions.solution_md: Large-angle scattering needs a concentrated positive nucleus.

marking_scheme.step: Explained by a small dense positive nucleus

questions.stem_md: Describe the observations of the alpha-particle scattering experiment on a thin gold foil and state three conclusions drawn from them.

answer.model_answer_md: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, a few were deflected through small or large angles, and very few rebounded almost along their original path. Conclusions: the atom is mostly empty space; the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny region; this nucleus is very dense and holds nearly all the mass, with electrons moving around it.

questions.solution_md: Three observations paired with three conclusions.

questions.stem_md: Which of these photons has the greatest energy?
questions.solution_md: $E = hc/\lambda$, so the photon of shortest wavelength has the greatest energy — violet, 410 nm, option (c).

questions.stem_md: When the electron of a hydrogen atom falls from n = 3 to n = 2, the line emitted belongs to the:

options.text_md: Balmer series, in the visible region
Lyman series, in the ultraviolet region
Paschen series, in the infrared region
Balmer series, in the ultraviolet region

questions.solution_md: The series is named by the level the electron lands on: n = 2 is the Balmer series, whose first lines lie in the visible region — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The ratio of the energies of photons of wavelength 300 nm and 600 nm is:
The wavenumber of light of wavelength 500 nm is:
questions.solution_md: $\bar{\nu} = 1/\lambda = 1 / (5.0 \times 10^{-7}) = 2.0 \times 10^{6}$, in m⁻¹ — option (a). (b) is the wavelength itself and (d) is the frequency in Hz.

questions.stem_md: Which arrangement lists radiations in order of increasing energy per photon?

options.text_md: radio waves < microwaves < visible light < X-rays
X-rays < visible light < microwaves < radio waves
microwaves < radio waves < X-rays < visible light
visible light < radio waves < X-rays < microwaves

questions.solution_md: Energy rises with frequency: radio waves have the lowest frequency, then microwaves, visible light and X-rays — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Light of frequency below the threshold frequency of a metal is made much more intense. As a result:

options.text_md: electrons are emitted with greater kinetic energy
more electrons are emitted, each with the same kinetic energy as before
electrons are emitted after a delay

questions.solution_md: Each photon is too weak to free an electron, and electrons do not pool energy from several photons, so no emission occurs however intense the light — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The radius of the second Bohr orbit of hydrogen is (take $r_n = 52.9\,n^2$ pm):
questions.solution_md: $r_2 = 52.9 \times 2^2 = 212$ pm — option (b). (d) is the radius for n = 3.

questions.stem_md: For the hydrogen atom, the ratio $E_3 : E_2$ of the energies of the third and second Bohr levels is:
A sample of excited hydrogen atoms has electrons in n = 4. The maximum number of different spectral lines that can be emitted as they fall to lower levels is:

**Assertion (A):** The line spectrum of hydrogen consists of discrete lines rather than a continuous band.

**Reason (R):** A hydrogen atom contains only one electron.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true, and R is true, but R is not the reason: lines are discrete because the electron has only certain allowed (quantised) energies, so photons emitted have only certain energies — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Doubling the intensity of light whose frequency is above the threshold frequency doubles the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.
questions.solution_md: False. Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons and hence the number of photoelectrons; the maximum kinetic energy depends only on frequency.

questions.stem_md: The series of lines in the hydrogen spectrum that lies in the visible region is the ___ series.
questions.solution_md: The **Balmer** series (transitions to n = 2) lies in the visible region.

questions.stem_md: An FM radio station broadcasts at a frequency of $98.4\ \text{MHz}$. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves in metres. ($c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{\nu} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{9.84 \times 10^{7}} = 3.05$ m, using $98.4\ \text{MHz} = 9.84 \times 10^{7}$ Hz.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the energy, in kJ, carried by one mole of photons of blue light of wavelength $450\ \text{nm}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $N_\text{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: One photon: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{4.50 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.42 \times 10^{-19}$ J. One mole: $4.42 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 2.66 \times 10^{5}$ J, and dividing by 1000: $2.66 \times 10^{5} / 1000 = 266$ kJ.

marking_scheme.step: Converts to kJ: 266 kJ per mole

questions.stem_md: Light of frequency $7.2 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$ falls on a metal surface whose threshold frequency is $4.8 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons, in units of $10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)

Calculate the wavelength, in nm, of the line emitted when the electron in a hydrogen atom falls from $n = 4$ to $n = 2$. ($E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}/n^2$ J, $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: $\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,(1/4 - 1/16) = 4.088 \times 10^{-19}$ J. $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{4.088 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 486 \times 10^{-9}$ m $= 486$ nm (blue-green, Balmer).

questions.stem_md: The radius of the $n$th Bohr orbit of a hydrogen-like ion of atomic number $Z$ is $r_n = 52.9\,n^2/Z$ pm. Calculate the radius of the second orbit of $\ce{He+}$, in pm.
questions.solution_md: $r_2 = 52.9 \times 2^2 / 2 = 105.8$ pm $\approx 106$ pm, half the radius of the second orbit of hydrogen (212 pm) because the nuclear charge is doubled.

questions.stem_md: A helium-neon laser of power $3.0\ \text{mW}$ emits light of wavelength $632.8\ \text{nm}$. Calculate the number of photons emitted per second, in units of $10^{15}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$; $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J s}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: Energy of one photon: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{6.328 \times 10^{-7}} = 3.14 \times 10^{-19}$ J. Power $= 3.0 \times 10^{-3}$ J s⁻¹, so photons per second $= \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{-3}}{3.14 \times 10^{-19}} = 9.55 \times 10^{15}$; in units of $10^{15}$: $9.55 \times 10^{15} / 10^{15} = 9.55$.

questions.stem_md: A metal emits no photoelectrons when exposed to a very intense beam of red light, but emits electrons immediately with a weak beam of ultraviolet light. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Each electron absorbs a single photon, and a photon of red light has less energy than the work function of the metal, so no electron is freed however many photons arrive. Ultraviolet photons have a higher frequency and carry more than the threshold energy, so each one can eject an electron at once.

questions.solution_md: Photon energy depends on frequency; threshold frequency decides emission.

marking_scheme.step: Red photons are below the threshold energy
Ultraviolet photons exceed it, so emission is immediate

questions.stem_md: Why does the emission spectrum of atomic hydrogen consist of separate lines instead of a continuous band of colours?

answer.model_answer_md: In Bohr’s model the electron can occupy only certain allowed energy levels. When it falls from a higher level to a lower one it emits a photon whose energy equals the difference between the two levels. Only particular energy differences exist, so only particular wavelengths appear as lines.

questions.solution_md: Quantised levels give fixed energy differences.

marking_scheme.step: Only certain energy levels are allowed
Photon energy equals the level difference: discrete wavelengths

questions.stem_md: State two limitations of Bohr’s model of the atom.

answer.model_answer_md: Bohr’s model cannot explain the spectra of atoms with more than one electron, nor the splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic or electric field. It also treats the electron only as a particle moving in an exact orbit, ignoring its wave nature and violating the uncertainty principle.

questions.solution_md: Any two of: many-electron atoms, line splitting, wave nature, uncertainty principle.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the postulates of Bohr’s model of the hydrogen atom.

(b) Using $E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}/n^2$ J, calculate the energy released and the wavelength of the photon when the electron falls from n = 3 to n = 1 ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹).

(c) Name the series to which this line belongs and the region of the spectrum.

answer.model_answer_md: Bohr’s postulates: the electron moves in fixed circular stationary orbits without radiating; each orbit has a definite energy and angular momentum $m_\text{e}vr = nh/2\pi$; energy is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits, $\Delta E = h\nu$. (b) The energy released is the difference between the two levels: $\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,(1/1 - 1/9) = 1.94 \times 10^{-18}$ J. The wavelength follows from $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.94 \times 10^{-18}} \approx 1.02 \times 10^{-7}$ m, that is 102 nm. (c) The electron lands on n = 1, so this is a line of the Lyman series, which lies in the ultraviolet region of the spectrum.

questions.solution_md: Three postulates; ΔE for 3→1; λ = hc/ΔE; Lyman, ultraviolet.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
The hydrogen discharge tube shows four visible lines. Their wavelengths are measured as follows. ($R_\text{H} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$)

| Line | Wavelength / nm |
|---|---|
| 1 | 656.3 |
| 2 | 486.1 |
| 3 | 434.0 |
| 4 | 410.2 |

All four lines arise from transitions that end on the same lower level.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) Balmer series

**(b)** The electron falls from n = 4 to n = 2, which fits the Rydberg formula.

**(c)** (i) The series limit corresponds to an electron falling from $n_2 = \infty$ to n = 2, which gives the shortest wavelength: $\bar{\nu} = R_\text{H}/4 = 1.097 \times 10^{7}/4 = 2.74 \times 10^{6}$ m⁻¹, so $\lambda = 1/\bar{\nu} = 3.65 \times 10^{-7}$ m, that is about 365 nm, which lies in the ultraviolet region.

**OR** (ii) The energy levels of hydrogen crowd closer together as n increases, because the energy varies as one over n squared. The differences between the upper levels and n = 2 therefore change less and less, so successive lines lie closer and converge on the series limit.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Lines in the visible region (410 to 656 nm) that end on n = 2 form the Balmer series — option (b). The Lyman series is ultraviolet and Paschen and Pfund are infrared.

**(b)** $1/\lambda = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\,(1/4 - 1/16) = 2.057 \times 10^{6}$ m⁻¹, giving $\lambda = 486$ nm: n = 4.

**(c)** (i) Take n₂ = ∞ in the Rydberg formula.

(ii) Energy levels converge as n increases.

children.stem_md: These four lines belong to the:

children.stem_md: From which level does the electron fall to produce line 2 (486.1 nm)?

Lines converge to the series limit

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md: A photocell uses a metal plate whose threshold wavelength is $600\ \text{nm}$ (illustrative value). The plate is illuminated with violet light of wavelength $400\ \text{nm}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$)

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) Electrons are emitted, because the photon energy exceeds the threshold energy.

**(b)** The threshold frequency is $\nu_0 = \dfrac{c}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{6.00 \times 10^{-7}} = 5.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

**(c)** (i) The energy of a violet photon is $hc/\lambda = 4.97 \times 10^{-19}$ J and the threshold energy is $hc/\lambda_0 = 3.31 \times 10^{-19}$ J. The maximum kinetic energy of an electron is the difference: $4.97 \times 10^{-19} - 3.31 \times 10^{-19} = 1.66 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

**OR** (ii) Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons and so the number of electrons emitted per second, but the maximum kinetic energy is unchanged. Red light of 700 nm has a wavelength longer than the threshold, so its photons are too weak and no electrons are emitted.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** A shorter wavelength means a higher frequency and more energy per photon, above the threshold for 600 nm — option (a).

**(b)** Threshold frequency from the threshold wavelength.

**(c)** (i) Photon energy minus threshold energy.

(ii) Intensity changes number; frequency changes kinetic energy.

children.stem_md: What happens when the violet light falls on the plate?

options.text_md: Electrons are emitted, because the photon energy exceeds the threshold energy.
No electrons are emitted, because 400 nm is shorter than 600 nm.
Electrons are emitted only after the plate warms up.
Electrons are emitted only if the light is made more intense.

children.solution_md: A shorter wavelength means a higher frequency and more energy per photon, above the threshold for 600 nm — option (a).

children.stem_md: Calculate the threshold frequency of the metal.

answer.model_answer_md: The threshold frequency is $\nu_0 = \dfrac{c}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{6.00 \times 10^{-7}} = 5.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

children.solution_md: Threshold frequency from the threshold wavelength.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron.

answer.model_answer_md: The energy of a violet photon is $hc/\lambda = 4.97 \times 10^{-19}$ J and the threshold energy is $hc/\lambda_0 = 3.31 \times 10^{-19}$ J. The maximum kinetic energy of an electron is the difference: $4.97 \times 10^{-19} - 3.31 \times 10^{-19} = 1.66 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): State what happens to the number and the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons if the intensity of the violet light is doubled, and if red light of 700 nm is used instead.

answer.model_answer_md: Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons and so the number of electrons emitted per second, but the maximum kinetic energy is unchanged. Red light of 700 nm has a wavelength longer than the threshold, so its photons are too weak and no electrons are emitted.

alternatives.solution_md: Intensity changes number; frequency changes kinetic energy.

questions.stem_md: An electron and a proton move with the same speed. Which statement about their de Broglie wavelengths is correct?

options.text_md: The proton has the longer wavelength because its mass is larger.
Both have the same wavelength because the speed is the same.
Neither has a wavelength because they are particles.
The electron has the longer wavelength because its mass is smaller.

questions.solution_md: $\lambda = h/mv$: for equal speed, the smaller mass gives the larger wavelength; the electron is about 1800 times lighter — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The uncertainty principle can be ignored for a moving cricket ball because:

options.text_md: a ball has no wave nature at all
the minimum uncertainty in its velocity is extremely small compared with its actual velocity
Planck’s constant is zero for large objects
a ball always moves at an exactly known speed

questions.solution_md: $\Delta v \ge h/(4\pi m \Delta x)$ is of the order $10^{-31}$ m s⁻¹ for a ball, utterly negligible — option (b). (a) is false: all matter has a wavelength, but it is unobservable for large objects.

questions.stem_md: If the speed of a moving electron is doubled, its de Broglie wavelength:
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = h/mv$, so $\lambda \propto 1/v$; doubling the speed halves the wavelength — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The de Broglie wavelength of a moving cricket ball cannot be detected.

**Reason (R):** A cricket ball has no wave nature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the wavelength is about 10⁻³⁴ m. R is false: all moving matter has a wavelength, but it is far too small to observe for a large object — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The principle stating that the position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known exactly is the ___ uncertainty principle.
questions.solution_md: This is the **Heisenberg** uncertainty principle.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at $2.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, in pm. ($m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$, $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)

marking_scheme.step: Uses λ = h/mv with SI units

questions.stem_md: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a cricket ball of mass $0.16\ \text{kg}$ moving at $40\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, in units of $10^{-34}\ \text{m}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = h/mv = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} / (0.16 \times 40) = 1.04 \times 10^{-34}$ m, so in units of $10^{-34}$ m: $1.04 \times 10^{-34} / 10^{-34} = 1.04$. This is far smaller than any atom or nucleus, so it cannot be observed.

questions.stem_md: The position of an electron is known to within $1.0 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$. Calculate the minimum uncertainty in its speed, in units of $10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$)

(a) State de Broglie’s relation and explain why the wave nature of matter is not observed for a cricket ball but is important for an electron.

(b) State Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle and write its mathematical form.

(c) Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a proton moving at $3.0 \times 10^{5}$ m s⁻¹ ($m_\text{p} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s).

answer.model_answer_md: de Broglie: a moving particle has wavelength $\lambda = h/mv$. For a cricket ball, the mass is large, so $\lambda$ is about $10^{-34}$ m, far too small to detect; for an electron the small mass gives a wavelength of the order of atomic dimensions, so wave behaviour is significant. Heisenberg: it is impossible to know exactly and simultaneously both the position and momentum of a microscopic particle, with $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge h/4\pi$. (c) $\lambda = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} / (1.673 \times 10^{-27} \times 3.0 \times 10^{5}) = 1.32 \times 10^{-12}$ m, about 1.3 pm.

questions.stem_md: State de Broglie’s relation. An electron and a proton move at the same speed. Find the ratio of their wavelengths and say which has the shorter wavelength. ($m_\text{p}/m_\text{e} \approx 1836$)

answer.model_answer_md: de Broglie’s relation is $\lambda = h/mv$: a moving particle of mass $m$ and speed $v$ behaves as a wave of this wavelength. At equal speed $\lambda \propto 1/m$, so $\lambda_\text{e}/\lambda_\text{p} = m_\text{p}/m_\text{e} \approx 1836$. The electron has a wavelength about 1836 times longer, so the proton, being heavier, has the shorter wavelength.

questions.stem_md: The number of radial nodes in a 3p orbital is:
questions.solution_md: Radial nodes $= n - l - 1 = 3 - 1 - 1 = 1$ — option (b). The orbital also has $l = 1$ angular node.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following sets of quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ) is **not** allowed?
questions.solution_md: l can take values from 0 to n − 1. For n = 2 the maximum is l = 1, so l = 2 is not allowed — option (c). The other sets obey l < n and |mₗ| ≤ l.

questions.stem_md: The total number of orbitals in the shell with n = 3 is:
questions.solution_md: Orbitals $= n^2 = 9$ (one 3s, three 3p and five 3d) — option (b). (d) is the number of electrons, $2n^2$.

options.text_md: 3 radial nodes and no angular node
4 radial nodes and no angular node
no radial node and 3 angular nodes

questions.solution_md: For 4s, $l = 0$: radial nodes $= 4 - 0 - 1 = 3$ and angular nodes $= l = 0$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The three 2p orbitals of an isolated atom have different energies.
questions.solution_md: False. The three 2p orbitals differ only in orientation, so they are degenerate (equal in energy) in an isolated atom.

questions.stem_md: The subshell with azimuthal quantum number l = 2 is called the ___ subshell.
questions.solution_md: l = 2 corresponds to the **d** subshell (s, p, d, f for 0, 1, 2, 3).

Size and energy of the shell

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an orbit in Bohr’s model and an orbital in the quantum mechanical model.

answer.model_answer_md: An orbit is a definite circular path at a fixed distance from the nucleus, along which Bohr pictured the electron moving. An orbital is a region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is high; it has no definite path and holds at most two electrons.

questions.solution_md: Path versus probability region.

questions.stem_md: For n = 4, list the possible values of l and give the number of orbitals in each subshell.

answer.model_answer_md: For n = 4, l can be 0, 1, 2 and 3. The subshells 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f therefore contain 1, 3, 5 and 7 orbitals, using 2l + 1 orbitals per subshell, giving 16 orbitals in all, which equals n squared.

questions.solution_md: l from 0 to n − 1; 2l + 1 orbitals.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the four quantum numbers and state the property of an electron each describes, with the allowed values.

(b) Find the number of orbitals and the maximum number of electrons in the shell n = 3, and list the quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ) of the 3p orbitals.

(c) Draw or describe the shapes of s and p orbitals and state the number of nodes in a 2s orbital.

answer.model_answer_md: n = 1, 2, 3 … gives the shell, size and energy; l = 0 to n − 1 gives the subshell and shape (s, p, d, f); mₗ = −l to +l gives the orientation; mₛ = +½ or −½ gives the spin. (b) For n = 3, l = 0, 1, 2 give $1 + 3 + 5 = 9$ orbitals and $2 \times 9 = 18$ electrons. The 3p orbitals have (3, 1, −1), (3, 1, 0) and (3, 1, +1). (c) An s orbital is spherical; a p orbital is a dumbbell with two lobes and a nodal plane through the nucleus. A 2s orbital has $2 - 0 - 1 = 1$ radial node and no angular node.

questions.solution_md: Four numbers with ranges; 9 orbitals, 18 electrons; shapes; one node for 2s.

| Set | n | l | mₗ | mₛ |

| A | 3 | 2 | −1 | +½ |
| B | 2 | 2 | 0 | +½ |

**(b)** It describes an electron in the 3d subshell.

**(c)** (i) Set B is not permitted because l must lie between 0 and n − 1, so for n = 2 the value l = 2 cannot occur. Set C is not permitted because mₗ must lie between −l and +l, so for l = 1 the value mₗ = 2 is impossible.

**OR** (ii) For the 3d orbital, radial nodes are 3 − 2 − 1 = 0 and angular nodes equal l = 2, so it has no radial node and two angular nodes.

**(b)** n = 3 and l = 2: 3d.

questions.stem_md: The ground-state electronic configuration of copper (Z = 29) is:
questions.solution_md: Copper is an exception: a completely filled 3d subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves to 3d, giving [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ — option (d). (a) is the configuration expected from the simple filling order.

questions.stem_md: The number of unpaired electrons in the Fe³⁺ ion (Z = 26) is:
questions.solution_md: Fe is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6 4s^2$. Fe³⁺ loses the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron: $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$, with one electron in each of the five 3d orbitals — 5 unpaired, option (a). (b) is the number for neutral Fe.

questions.stem_md: According to the (n + l) rule, the correct order of increasing energy is:
questions.solution_md: $(n + l)$: 4s = 4, 3d = 5, 4p = 5. 4s is lowest; 3d and 4p tie at 5, so the one with lower $n$ (3d) is lower — option (c).

**Assertion (A):** Chromium has the configuration [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ rather than [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².

**Reason (R):** A half-filled subshell has extra stability due to symmetrical distribution and greater exchange energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Moving one 4s electron to 3d gives a half-filled 3d subshell, which is extra stable for the stated reasons; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins.

**Reason (R):** Hund’s rule states that electrons pair up in an orbital before occupying other orbitals of the same subshell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (Pauli exclusion principle). R is false: Hund’s rule says electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly before pairing — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The principle that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers is the ___ exclusion principle.
questions.solution_md: This is the **Pauli** exclusion principle.

questions.stem_md: State Pauli’s exclusion principle and use it to show that the shell n = 2 can hold at most 8 electrons.

answer.model_answer_md: No two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital, which has fixed n, l and mₗ, can hold at most two electrons with opposite spins. The shell n = 2 has four orbitals (one 2s and three 2p), so it holds at most 2 × 4 = 8 electrons.

questions.solution_md: Two per orbital times four orbitals.

questions.stem_md: State Hund’s rule. Draw the orbital box diagram for the 2p subshell of nitrogen and of oxygen and give the number of unpaired electrons in each.

answer.model_answer_md: Hund’s rule: in a subshell of degenerate orbitals, electrons occupy separate orbitals singly with parallel spins before any pairing occurs. Nitrogen has 2p³: three boxes each with one up arrow, so three unpaired electrons. Oxygen has 2p⁴: the first box holds an up and a down arrow and the other two boxes one up arrow each, so two unpaired electrons.

questions.solution_md: Singly first; N has 3 unpaired, O has 2.

questions.stem_md: Write the ground-state configurations of chromium (Z = 24) and copper (Z = 29) and explain why they differ from the order predicted by the Aufbau principle.

answer.model_answer_md: Chromium is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1$ and copper is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1$, not $3d^4 4s^2$ and $3d^9 4s^2$. The 3d and 4s energies are close, so moving one 4s electron into 3d gives a half-filled (Cr) or completely filled (Cu) 3d subshell. These arrangements are extra stable because of their symmetry and the larger exchange energy.

questions.solution_md: Two configurations; half-filled and filled subshell stability.

questions.stem_md: Write the ground-state configurations of Fe, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ and explain which electrons are lost first when iron forms cations.

answer.model_answer_md: Fe (Z = 26) is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6 4s^2$; Fe²⁺ is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6$ and Fe³⁺ is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$. In forming cations the electrons of the outermost shell, those with the highest $n$, are lost first, so the two 4s electrons leave before any 3d electron. Fe³⁺ then has a half-filled, stable 3d subshell.

questions.solution_md: Highest-n electrons leave first.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the Aufbau principle, Pauli’s exclusion principle and Hund’s rule.

(b) Write the electronic configuration of sulfur (Z = 16) and of the sulfide ion, and give the number of unpaired electrons in sulfur.

(c) Write the configurations of chromium and copper and explain why they are exceptions.

answer.model_answer_md: Aufbau: electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy, that is increasing $n + l$. Pauli: no two electrons in an atom have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin. Hund: degenerate orbitals are filled singly with parallel spins before pairing. (b) S is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^4$; $\ce{S^2-}$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6$. The 3p⁴ subshell has one pair and two single electrons, so sulfur has 2 unpaired electrons. (c) Cr is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1$ and Cu is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1$; half-filled and filled 3d subshells are extra stable because of symmetry and exchange energy.

questions.solution_md: Three rules; S and S²⁻; two unpaired; Cr and Cu.

A student writes the ground-state configurations of three atoms in a test.

| Copper (Z = 29) | [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s² |
